newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's Liberals slip further - Reuters poll.
newsitem.headline: Canada's Liberals slip further - Reuters poll.

text.p: Support for Canada's ruling Liberal Party has eroded further, throwing into doubt whether it can win another outright parliamentary majority in the June 2 election, a new Reuters poll released on Wednesday showed.

The poll conducted for Reuters by Zogby International, the fourth in a series of five daily tracking polls, showed support for Prime Minister Jean Chretien's Liberals falling to 39.7 percent -- below the key 40 percent level for the first time.
"If the tracking poll trends continue, Chretien may not win a majority," pollster John Zogby said.
"Forty percent is the generally accepted benchmark level for whether or not the Liberals will have a firm majority," Zogby said in a telephone interview.
However, he did not rule out a Liberal majority even if the party won less than 40 percent of the vote next Monday.
"It's got to go riding (electoral district) by riding," he said.
Chretien, although not commenting directly on polls, voiced confidence on Wednesday that the Liberals would regain their majority.
"We are very confident we will form a government...we will have a majority government..." Chretien told reporters after a campaign stop in Edmonton, Alberta.
In the 1993 election, the Liberals won 177 of the 295 parliamentary seats, with 41 percent of the vote.
Even so, Canada's currency and bond markets were unnerved for the second straight day on Wednesday by poll-driven concerns that the Liberals might fall short of a majority in Parliament.
The Canadian dollar was hit by pre-election jitters, losing almost half a U.S. cent on Tuesday and continued to hover around 72.28 U.S. cents on Wednesday.

"Activity is a lot more poll driven because the currency had been priced for a best-case scenario outcome to the election (Liberal majority)," said Rob Palombi, senior analyst at economics firm MMS International in Toronto.
In Canada's electoral system, the candidate that wins the most votes in each district is elected to the House of Commons. The leader of the party with the most seats becomes prime minister.
Support for the Liberals has fallen steadily since Chretien called an election at the end of April, 18 months before he was constitutionally required to do so.

A Reuters-Zogby poll on May 4 put the Liberals at 47.6 percent, falling to 45.4 percent on May 16 and to 43.8 percent on May 25. The slide continued through this week, with Liberal support sliding to 39.7 percent on Wednesday from 40.7 on Tuesday and 42.2 percent on Monday.
The latest poll surveyed 1,096 voters from May 25 to May 27, with a 3.1 percentage point margin of error, 19 times out of 20.
The Conservatives' support held steady in Wednesday's poll at 21.5 percent, with the right-wing Reform Party slipping to 17.5 percent from Tuesday's 18.8 percent and Monday's 19.3 percent.
The left-wing New Democrats held their 9.3 percent support and the secessionist Bloc Quebecois was virtually unchanged at 6.7 percent.

The Liberals were strongest in vote-rich Ontario, where they had 55 percent in the latest Reuters-Zogby poll, up from 49 percent on Tuesday. The Conservatives were second in Ontario at about 21 percent, followed by Reform at 14 percent.
"If Reform continues to grow in Ontario, this could be a heavy blow to the Tories (Conservatives)," Zogby said.
In French-speaking Quebec, the Bloc Quebecois was neck and neck with the Liberals and the Conservatives, the Reuters poll showed.
The Bloc Quebecois won 54 of Quebec's 75 seats in 1993, enough to form the official opposition in Parliament.
Reform continued to dominate in Alberta and British Columbia, while the Conservatives gained support in Quebec and the Maritimes.
